candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the archive bytes: POST /command/core/import-project accepts multipart/form-data with a file field (or a "url" field, which the server fetches itself), so any tar or tar.gz containing entries such as "../../.../target" can be delivered. Entry names are taken verbatim from the archive and flow unmodified into the file path. The command is registered (controller.js:65) and, like all core commands in this snapshot, has no authentication, CSRF token, or Origin/Referer validation (none of Command.java, RefineServlet.java, or the webapp Ajax helpers contain such checks), so the endpoint is reachable both by a client that can connect to the OpenRefine port and, if the browser can reach it, via a cross-site form post.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) ImportingUtilities.allocateFile (lines 437-460) and its callers explodeArchive (lines 614-683) do enforce a traversal check, so the bug is not present in the generic importer path; project import simply bypasses that helper. (2) No validation appears in ImportProjectCommand, in the abstract ProjectManager.importProject (lines 165-172), or in getProjectDir; no subclass overrides importProject/untar. (3) Only POST is accepted, but the UI form (import-project-ui.html) and any HTTP client can post the archive, and there is no auth/CSRF/origin control in RefineServlet/Command. (4) For the file-fetch branch the tar stream is attacker-controlled via the url field, still parsed by the unchecked untar. (5) The tar implementation (org.apache.tools.tar, Ant 1.8.0 per main/pom.xml lines 333-337) is not part of the snapshot; per the Ant API it strips only leading slashes and preserves ".." segments, so the traversal is expected to survive, but this dependency behavior was not verified from repository source. (6) No test sources are present to show an intended containment check.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file creation or overwrite outside the project directory with the privileges of the OpenRefine process. An attacker can corrupt or replace user files, configuration/startup files, or the application's own files (integrity/availability impact), and arbitrary write primitives of this kind can plausibly be escalated to code execution (for example by overwriting files that OpenRefine or the user later loads or executes). It also allows planting files into other project/workspace locations.
candidates.prerequisites: Network access to the OpenRefine HTTP endpoint (default binding is localhost, but server/LAN/reverse-proxy deployments expose it) or the ability to make a victim's browser issue the multipart POST; the OpenRefine process must have write permission on the target path (normally true for the user's own files, the workspace directory, and a self-managed installation directory).
candidates.root_cause: FileProjectManager.untar() derives the extraction destination directly from the archive entry name (new File(destDir, tarEntry.getName())) and writes it via FileOutputStream after mkdirs on the parent, without verifying that the normalized/canonical path stays inside destDir. Entry names containing "../" therefore escape workspace/<id>.project and let the archive create or overwrite arbitrary files with the OpenRefine process's privileges. The parallel archive-extraction routine ImportingUtilities.allocateFile() applies exactly such a containment check (commented "For CVE-2018-19859, issue #1840"), so the same hardening was not applied to the project-archive import path.
candidates.title: Arbitrary file write via path traversal in tar extraction during project import (tar-slip in FileProjectManager.untar)
candidates.trace: controller.js:65 registers core/import-project -> ImportProjectCommand.doPost (line 64) -> internalImport (line 98) consumes the uploaded stream (lines 121-125) or the url field (lines 129-131, internalImportURL at line 134) and calls ProjectManager.singleton.importProject(projectID, stream, gziped) (lines 122/159) -> FileProjectManager.importProject (line 150) sets destDir = workspace/<id>.project (line 151) and calls untar (lines 154-159) -> untar loop (line 166): destEntry = new File(destDir, tarEntry.getName()) (line 167), parent.mkdirs() (line 171), then new FileOutputStream(destEntry) and tin.copyEntryContents(fout) (lines 177-179). No canonical/normalized containment test exists anywhere on this path, and no subclass overrides importProject/untar.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code executed). The exact name-normalization behavior of the Ant 1.8.0 TarEntry/TarInputStream classes could not be verified from the snapshot because the dependency is not included; the traversal claim assumes those names are passed through (standard Ant behavior). Also unverified: the deployment's bind address/reverse-proxy exposure, and whether a modern browser would allow the cross-site multipart POST to localhost (Private Network Access policies) if the server is only on the loopback interface. Impact escalation to code execution is plausible but not demonstrated.
candidates.weakness_type: Path traversal / unrestricted file write (CWE-22, CWE-73; "Zip Slip"/tar-slip)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the complete assigned snapshot (941 files, no files excluded by size/name/symlink filters): main/src Java core (commands and their registrations in main/webapp/modules/core/MOD-INF/controller.js, importing/importers, io/FileProjectManager/ProjectUtilities/ProjectMetadataUtilities, exporters, model/recon, expr/templating, util, ProjectManager/RefineServlet), main/webapp JS/HTML/config, and the database, gdata, jython, wikidata and other extensions. I used the P1 relation index (index_status complete, 941/941 files indexed, 0 missing; 13k syntactic edges / 505 facts) only for navigation, following the command-registration, call, containment and "security_call" hints into source text, and verified every claim against the read files. All call sites of TarInputStream/ZipInputStream getNextEntry, FileOutputStream and importProject/untar were enumerated; the unchecked project-import untar path is the only archive extraction loop lacking a containment check. The index provides no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability analysis, and no build or tests were run.
limitations: Static review only: no code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

Third-party dependency internals are absent from the snapshot (Ant 1.8.0 org.apache.tools.tar, Apache HttpClient, Jackson, Jetty, commons-fileupload), so their exact behavior (notably TarEntry name normalization) was inferred from call sites rather than verified here.

Webapp template files referenced by the code (e.g., error.vt used by Command/HttpUtilities) are not present in the snapshot, so server-side template rendering/escaping surfaces could not be inspected.
The snapshot contains no test sources, so intended invariants or regression tests for archive extraction could not be cross-checked.

Relation-index facts are syntactic navigation hints only; dynamic dispatch, reflection (e.g., RefineServlet.getClass/Class.forName paths), and complete data flow were assessed manually from source text and may be incomplete.
Deployment-specific facts (bind address, reverse-proxy exposure, OS path semantics for absolute or Windows-style archive entry names) were not empirically verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-Slip in generic import archive extraction (ImportingUtilities.explodeArchive)
rejected_leads.reason: Already hardened: every extracted entry goes through allocateFile (lines 437-460), which rejects paths escaping the raw-data directory (comment references CVE-2018-19859). No bypass found in that path.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal via the 'lang' parameter in LoadLanguageCommand.loadLanguage (line 117)
rejected_leads.reason: The user value is concatenated after the fixed prefix 'translation-' and before the fixed suffix '.json', so classic ../ payloads require a directory literally named 'translation-' (or 'translation-..') to exist; no practical traversal payload was identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Absence of CSRF/Origin/Referer protection on state-changing commands
rejected_leads.reason: Real hardening gap in this snapshot (no tokens found in Java or JS), and it can enable browser-driven delivery of the submitted issue, but by itself it is a missing defense rather than a distinct sink with attacker-controlled impact; retained as an exploitation prerequisite instead.

rejected_leads.lead: Unrestricted URL scheme in import-project URL import (file:// and other schemes, ImportProjectCommand.internalImportURL lines 134-163)
rejected_leads.reason: The fetched content is only parsed as a tar archive and there is no direct read-back/exfiltration sink, so SSRF/local-file impact is not established; it is subsumed by the submitted candidate as a delivery vector.

rejected_leads.lead: Database extension: hardcoded PBE key plus PBEWithMD5AndDES for saved JDBC passwords (DatabaseUtils line 56, SimpleTextEncryptor lines 49-55), and SavedConnectionCommand returning decrypted passwords to any requester
rejected_leads.reason: Weak secret storage/weak KDF and an information-disclosure surface, but exploitation requires local access to the saved-connections file or reaching the port, and stored DB credentials are user-supplied; impact is lower and less direct than the arbitrary file write.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF/outbound URL handling in reconciliation, fetch-URL columns, Wikitext/GData/Wikidata extensions
rejected_leads.reason: Outbound requests to user-configured endpoints are a designed feature of these components; no trust-boundary violation or data-exfiltration path was established from source, so these remain unconfirmed leads.

summary: OpenRefine 3.2-SNAPSHOT (941-file snapshot, full Java core + webapp + extensions). I traced the HTTP command layer, the importing/importers subsystem, project/workspace I/O, exporters, model/expr code, and the database/gdata/wikidata/jython extensions, prioritizing archive extraction, file-path sinks, URL fetching, and reflection. Strongest finding: project-archive import performs tar extraction without any path-containment check, giving an unauthenticated caller an arbitrary file write outside the project directory. The sibling archive path (ImportingUtilities.allocateFile) contains the explicit CVE-2018-19859 zip-slip guard, so this is an incomplete fix of the same bug class in a different sink. All observations are static; nothing was executed or confirmed at runtime.
